I need to decide on an auction bid for SHORT_LINE.

I have $546 and several mortgaged properties. The opponent has $225 and monopolies on orange and dark blue. I need to weigh these factors against the auction bid.

The opponent currently leads the auction at $30. I should bid $31 and raise by $1 each turn until I reach $99, then drop out. This maximizes liquidity while keeping the dark-blue houses affordable.

Mortgaging a winning Short Line would net $100 in cash. But owning a mortgaged railroad prevents rent collection, so I must decide if that trade-off is worthwhile.

The opponent is currently on SHORT_LINE. They likely landed there and declined to buy, triggering the auction. They already own B&O, so an unmortgaged Short Line would give them a second active railroad.

No retroactive rent applies if I win the auction while the opponent is already standing on the space. The opponent has already missed that landing opportunity.

The mortgage arbitrage is confirmed as positive expected value. A bid under $100 nets cash after the $100 mortgage, and unmortgaging costs $110. The opponent is matching my incremental bids, so I need to determine why they continue raising.

The opponent likely recognizes the same mortgage arbitrage, so both players have incentive to bid below $100. Beyond cash, owning Short Line would let me unmortgage all three railroads for $100 in rent, though Reading RR costs about $110 to unmortgage.

Unmortgaging all three railroads would cost $330 for only $100 in rent, so that is not a worthwhile immediate goal. The opponent already owns B&O mortgaged, which they could unmortgage to collect $50 from two active railroads. The mortgage arbitrage remains the dominant strategic value for both players.

Dropping out now would let the opponent buy Short Line for $30 and mortgage it for $100, gaining $70 in cash. That would strengthen them too much. I should keep bidding up to $99 so I can claim the arbitrage myself.

I should jump directly to $99. If the opponent bids $100, I drop and they pay $100 for a $100 mortgage, netting zero cash. That outcome is still preferable to them winning at a lower price.

I will bid incrementally to $99 rather than jumping straight there. This preserves the strategic endgame while taking fewer turns. I am now on Water Works and need to roll.

I cannot afford a dark-blue hit. Three houses on Park Place and Boardwalk would cost $1100 and $1400, but I only have $546. I must either raise cash or avoid those spaces.

Rolling a 2 from Water Works lands on Go to Jail. A 3 lands on Pacific Avenue, which is mortgaged and mine. A 4 lands on North Carolina Avenue, also mortgaged and mine. A 5 lands on Community Chest.

Rolling a 9 or 11 from Water Works lands on Park Place or Boardwalk, both costing $1100 and $1400 respectively. That is a 16.7% chance of bankruptcy with only $546 cash. I need to raise the shortfall by mortgaging States Avenue for $70 or Ventnor for $130.

I cannot mortgage properties that already have houses. Selling the four houses on Oriental, three on Vermont, and three on Connecticut would raise $250, but that would destroy my rent income. I could also sell States Avenue for $70 and Ventnor for $130, adding another $200. Combined with my $546 cash, I would still only have $746, which is short of the $1100 needed to survive a dark-blue hit.

Even after selling all light blue houses, I would still lack $104 to survive a Park Place hit. The auction bid of $31 plus the $100 mortgage would net only $69 in cash, leaving me with $615 total. I am now considering whether mortgaging properties after selling houses could bridge the remaining gap.

Selling houses and mortgaging the light blue properties would raise about $160, giving me $1156 total. That covers a Park Place hit but not Boardwalk. I would have no rent income left.

The opponent is on SHORT_LINE with $225. Their next roll from there could land on Park Place or Boardwalk, both of which they own.

A roll of 12 from Short Line lands on Oriental Avenue with four houses, costing $400. The opponent has only $225, so they would need to raise about $175. They could mortgage Baltic Avenue for $30 or Kentucky Avenue for $110.

The opponent can mortgage Illinois for $120, giving them $485 total. That covers the $400 Oriental rent. I will continue bidding to $99 because the arbitrage raises cash and slightly improves my survival odds.

Dropping out now would let the opponent buy Short Line for $30, mortgage it for $100, and net $70 in cash. That would make them safer against my light-blue rents. I should bid $31 now and keep raising until $99. If I jump straight to $99, I deny them that $70 profit even if they match.

I realized that bidding $31 instead of $99 could let me win at a lower price. If the opponent only wanted the railroad cheap and would have dropped at $40, I would gain $69 in cash rather than just $1. This makes the incremental approach more valuable than jumping straight to $99.

The opponent has matched every bid from $1 to $30, so they appear committed to reaching $99. If they are truly committed, jumping straight to $99 now saves 68 decision rounds without changing the final outcome. The incremental approach only matters if they would drop out early.
